stops.name: Independence Hall
stops.teaser: Where a country was argued into existence.
stops.map: Independence Hall, 520 Chestnut St, Philadelphia, PA
stops.clue: Find the red brick State House with a white steeple on Chestnut Street in Independence National Historical Park.
stops.safety: Interior visits may need timed tickets and security screening. Stay on the walkways and follow park ranger directions.

then.label: The Declaration
then.line: The Declaration of Independence was adopted here in 1776.

now.head: Today
now.label: The hall today
now.line: The red brick State House is the centerpiece of Independence National Historical Park.

story: The building was built from 1732 to 1753 as the Pennsylvania State House. Edmund Woolley and Andrew Hamilton designed it.
The Declaration of Independence was adopted here on July 4, 1776. The U.S. Constitution was drafted here at the Constitutional Convention from May 25 to September 17, 1787, in the Assembly Room.
The original wooden steeple rotted and was removed in 1781. A new, more elaborate steeple by William Strickland was added in 1828. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
stops.fact: Two of the country's founding documents were created in one room.
stops.disputed: Nothing big is disputed here. The common mistake is thinking the steeple is the original.

claims.t: The Declaration of Independence was adopted at Independence Hall in 1776.
The steeple on Independence Hall today is the original from the 1700s.
claims.why: The original wooden steeple was removed in 1781. A new one was added in 1828.

stops.name: Liberty Bell
stops.teaser: A cracked bell with a myth bigger than its crack.
stops.map: Liberty Bell Center, 526 Market St, Philadelphia, PA
stops.clue: Look across from Independence Hall for the Liberty Bell Center. Inside is a large bell with a big crack.
stops.safety: Expect a security line and crowds. The exhibit is indoors and the bell is behind a barrier, so look but do not touch.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.prompt: Read the lettering on the bell. Which word is in capital letters?
q.hint: The bell is named for it.
q.verify: Wikipedia gives the inscription as "Proclaim LIBERTY Throughout all the Land," from Leviticus 25:10. Check the lettering on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.label: Cast in London
then.line: The bell was cast in 1752, cracked, and was recast in Philadelphia.

now.head: Today
now.label: The bell today
now.line: The bell sits in the Liberty Bell Center, across from Independence Hall.

story: The bell was cast in 1752 in London by Lester and Pack, later the Whitechapel Bell Foundry. It cracked on its first strike in Philadelphia. John Pass and John Stow recast it in 1752 and 1753, adding copper. The first recast sounded bad, so they did it again.
It weighs 2,080 pounds. The inscription comes from Leviticus 25:10. The famous crack formed between 1817 and 1846, most likely near the end of that span.
Abolitionists called it the Liberty Bell in the 1830s. It moved to the Liberty Bell Center in October 2003.
stops.fact: The "Liberty Bell" name came from abolitionists, not the Founders.
stops.disputed: The legend that the bell rang for the Declaration on July 4, 1776 lacks evidence. It most likely rang on July 8, when the Declaration was first read publicly, but no account from the time confirms it.

claims.t: The words on the Liberty Bell come from the Bible, from Leviticus.
claims.why: Wikipedia: the inscription is from Leviticus 25:10.

claims.t: The Liberty Bell cracked while tolling for Chief Justice John Marshall's death in 1835.
claims.why: A common story, but the evidence is thin. The crack formed sometime between 1817 and 1846.

stops.name: Betsy Ross House
stops.teaser: A small house with a famous story that historians argue about.
stops.map: Betsy Ross House, 239 Arch St, Philadelphia, PA
stops.clue: In Old City, find a small brick house on Arch Street with a flag out front.
stops.safety: Arch Street sidewalks are narrow and busy. Keep to the sidewalk, and note the house is a small museum with limited space.

now.label: The house today

story: The front of the house was built around 1740. The stair hall and back section were added 10 to 20 years later.

Betsy Ross may have lived here from 1776, after her first husband John Ross died, until about 1779. But her living here is disputed. The best archival evidence suggests she lived in the house next door, which was later torn down.

The story that she designed and sewed the first flag traces to her relatives, especially her grandsons William and George Canby, and to the 1876 Centennial. Historians call these claims controversial. The house was restored in 1937 and given to the city in 1941.
stops.fact: The famous story is mostly a family legend from after her death.
stops.disputed: Whether she lived here or sewed the first flag is disputed. The house is real. The story is the argument.

claims.t: The front of the Betsy Ross House was built around 1740.
claims.why: Wikipedia: the front part dates to about 1740.

claims.t: Betsy Ross sewed the first American flag in this house.
claims.why: Historians call it controversial. The story comes from relatives, and she may have lived next door.

stops.name: Elfreth's Alley
stops.teaser: A tiny street older than the country, still full of people's homes.
stops.clue: In Old City, find a narrow lane of small brick row houses, near 2nd Street, just north of Arch.
stops.safety: People live here. Be quiet, stay out of doorways and private steps, and do not photograph inside windows. Cars and delivery drivers also use the lane.

now.head: Today
now.label: The alley today
now.line: The row houses are still homes, and the lane is a National Historic Landmark.

story: Elfreth's Alley was laid out between 1702 and 1704. Wikipedia gives 1703 as the founding date. It has 32 houses, built between 1703 and 1836.
Early residents were artisans, such as shipwrights, silver and pewter smiths, glassblowers and furniture builders.
The alley is called the nation's oldest residential street. It became a National Historic Landmark on October 9, 1960. Each June a Fete Day opens homes to visitors.
stops.fact: Real people still live in these houses today.
stops.disputed: "Oldest" is argued. The word "continuously inhabited" shows up in Wikipedia only in a footnote about other places with old houses, so check the exact wording whenever you read it.

claims.t: Elfreth's Alley has 32 houses built between 1703 and 1836.
Elfreth's Alley is the oldest continuously inhabited street in America.
claims.why: Wikipedia calls it the nation's oldest residential street. Other places also claim old homes, so the exact wording matters.
